transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-20 10:00 UTC - Duration 45m
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sofia (RiverMark MLOps), Marcus (RiverMark Platform), Liam (RiverMark SRE)
Links referenced: benchmark spreadsheet (internal) https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/rivermark-poc , security deck, dedicated pool config doc

Summary: quick review of last week's run, profiling results, plan to focus on TTFT (time-to-first-token) and streaming behavior, discuss kernel choices and sequence length tradeoffs.

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Sofia: Hi, Sofia here.
[00:10] Marcus: Marcus on platform.
[00:12] Liam: Liam, SRE.
[00:15] Priya: Priya from Redwood SE. Evan?
[00:17] Evan: Evan here. Cool. Quick agenda: recap last run, look at kernel probe, TTFT numbers, streaming, then next steps.

[00:40] Priya: Alright so the high level, last week we ran the mixed workload on your dev cluster with the default kernel selection. We saw median token latency good but TTFT was, uh, higher than expected — roughly 230ms median and 650ms 95th with cold KV state. Some of that looks like quantized kernel fallback on the longer sequences.
[01:05] Marcus: Yep, that's what we saw in our logs too, especially for sequences >256. 95th balloons.

[01:20] Sofia: Can you clarify what you mean by kernel fallback? Are we falling back to a generic kernel?
[01:24] Priya: Yeah so our runtime picks specialized kernels for attention and rotary operations, but for some model shapes and quantization modes it falls back to a slower reference kernel — that shows up as the TTFT spike. Sometimes transcription calls it "kernel fallback" or, uh, "kermel fallback" in the logs.

[01:50] Liam: Any chance this is due to batch sizing? We saw some bursts where batching didn't form quickly.
[01:55] Priya: Good call. Batching and streaming interact a lot. For TTFT-focused workloads you want minimal batching and streaming turned on so the first token flows immediately; but if you go too small you pay overhead per-request. We tuned the batch timeout to 20ms in the last run which helped median but not the tail.

[02:30] Evan: Quick show of numbers from the probe (Priya, feel free to correct me) - specialized kernel used ~70% of time on seq<=256, but for seq512 it drops to ~35% and the rest fell to the reference kernel which adds ~200-300ms.
[02:50] Priya: Correct. Also saw that the 4-bit quant path is slightly slower at startup due to dequant passes on first inference — warming cache helps.

[03:10] Marcus: Is that because of KV cache misses? We noticed cold-starts hit disk first then mem.
[03:16] Priya: It's more the kernel init + dequant step; KV cache misses add more on top if your prefix caching isn't warmed. For RiverMark's workload you have a lot of short prompts but irregular prefixes so warming is tricky.

[03:45] Sofia: Any quick wins to drop TTFT this week?
[03:48] Priya: A few: pre-warm by replaying hot prefixes (we can script that), enable streaming with chunked output so the model returns partial tokens faster, and force the runtime to prefer the specialized kernel for seq<=256 by adjusting kernel selection thresholds. Also consider reducing sequence length cap for inference to 256 if your use-case allows.

[04:20] Liam: Streaming — we're worried about consistency and token ordering if we chunk. Any risk?
[04:25] Priya: With Redwood streaming we send partial tokens as they're decoded, we maintain order. The main tradeoff is slightly higher resource usage and more small writes, but overall TTFT improves a lot. We had a customer drop median TTFT by ~120ms with streaming enabled. Note: streaming option is in the SDK and requires a small client change.

[05:00] Evan: On kernel choices — Priya, you mentioned running a kernel probe; can you summarize probe plan?
[05:05] Priya: Yep: we run a tight set of synthetic and real-request probes across sequence lengths 64/128/256/512, with quant modes 8-bit and 4-bit, and record kernel selection, first-token latency, and throughput. We'll upload CSVs and a short analysis. That surfaces the precise seq length where fallback happens.

[05:35] Marcus: Will that also show where attention kernel degrades? We've seen attention matmul become slow at certain batch shapes.
[05:42] Priya: It will, we capture kernel timings including attention, matmul and dequant. There's occasional mis-labeled metrics in the probe (autogen names) but we annotate.

[06:05] Sofia: Ok, about dedicated pool — your recommendation last week was try a small dedicated GPU pool to isolate noisy neighbors and test kernel preloading?
[06:12] Evan: Yup. Dedicated pool gives consistent latency and lets us preload models/kernels into GPU memory so TTFT drop is real. Cost tradeoff: you pay reserved capacity but you get much better 95th.

[06:25] Sofia: Do you have numbers on how much improvement?
[06:28] Priya: In our internal bench, moving to a small dedicated pool with preloaded model cut 95th by about 40% for similar load. But depends on your exact arrival pattern. We'll share the benchmark link.

[06:50] Liam: Any security/ops blockers for dedicated? We run in a VPC and need KMS integration for keys.
[06:56] Evan: Dedicated/Private supports KMS/HSM integrations; we'll attach the security doc. No showstoppers. You may need a small network allowlist change.

[07:15] Marcus: Back to sequence length — if we cap at 256, what happens to inference correctness? Some of our prompts are naturally longer.
[07:22] Priya: You can do prefix truncation heuristics or move longer ones to a background non-LLM path. For many customers the majority of interactive prompts are <256; longer batch jobs can be routed to a fallback model variant configured for throughput. We can create a routing policy that uses token-length to pick the model variant.

[07:50] Sofia: Routing policies — do we need to manage that in-app or can Redwood do it at the edge?
[07:55] Evan: Redwood runtime supports smart routing by policy. We can set a rule: if sequence_length>256 route to model-x-high-throughput else model-y-low-ttft. We'll include a sample policy.

[08:20] Priya: Quick note: there's occasional mis-transcriptions in your logs — e.g., "KV catch" instead of "KV cache" — don't worry it's just the auto-generator.

[08:32] Marcus: Haha noted.

[08:40] Priya: Ok practical plan for this week: 1) I run kernel probes and share raw CSV + short analysis by Friday; 2) Evan shares dedicated pool cost/throughput options + fallback policy doc; 3) RiverMark runs a 1k-sample streaming-enabled run and shares logs so we can compare tails.

[09:05] Sofia: On the 1k run — do you want any special headers or tracing tags?
[09:09] Priya: Yes add X-Request-Tag: rivermark-poc and enable the per-request tracing (we'll give curl snippet). That helps correlate which kernel was used per request.

[09:25] Marcus: For the streaming run we'll probably need to tweak client since we use a JS client. Work will be minor but I will confirm timeline.

[09:35] Evan: Anything else on troubleshooting?
[09:37] Liam: One more — cold-start CPU overhead looked high on model load spikes. Can we preload in dedicated?
[09:40] Priya: Yes we can pre-warm GPU and preload model artifacts into pinned memory on dedicated which reduces cold-start by ~200-400ms depending on model size.

[09:55] Evan: Alright let's recap: Priya - kernel probe (due Fri), Evan - cost/pricing + policy doc (due Sat), RiverMark - streaming run + logs (due Sat). We'll reconvene same time next week to review canary plan.

[10:10] Sofia: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[10:15] Meeting ends.
